newsitem.title: BELGIUM: West's catastrophe - nightmare in Zaire moves closer.
newsitem.headline: West's catastrophe - nightmare in Zaire moves closer.

text.p: The West's nightmare of a major catastrophe in the heart of Africa drew closer on Tuesday with the European Union warning a million people could die and Zaire accusing Rwanda of trying to carve out a Tutsi empire.
Emma Bonino, the European Union's aid chief, called for international action to stop the spreading conflict in eastern Zaire where government troops are battling Banyamulenge Tutsi fighters.
"The lives of one million people are in danger," she declared, accusing the world of standing aloof from the unfolding tragedy.
"For the moment, 500,000 people are missing," she added.

In Geneva, the U.N. refugee agency said about 600,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutus -- who fled other conflicts with Tutsis in their own countries -- were cut off from foreign aid in eastern Zaire, which the government in Kinshasa has placed under military rule.
The agency appealed to governments for satellite photographs to help track what was happening.
U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees spokeswoman Ruth Marshall also reported fresh fighting near the teeming refugee camps on Rwanda's borders which could set off a new exodus.

Zaire's Interior Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda accused Rwanda's Tutsi-led government in Kigali, which itself swept to power in 1994 to end a Hutu-inspired genocide of Tutsis, of involvement in the fighting.

He told Belgian radio Kigali's masterplan was to create a Tutsi super-state out of parts of eastern Zaire, Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi -- a move which could destabilise several governments across a vast swathe of Africa.
"A state in which there could not be any inter-ethnic problem whatsoever, a Tutsi-land," he told Belgian RTBF radio in Kinshasa.
Kamanda said Hutus, who make up the majority in both Rwanda and Burundi and whose refugee camps are partly blamed for destabilising the Great Lakes region, would be driven deeper into Zaire.
"They want to drive into the interior all those considered non-Tutsis," he added.

On Monday, Rwanda paraded 10 alleged Rwandan army "prisoners of war", saying they were seized trying to sabotage the airport at Bukavu, the frontline of fighting between Zaire's army and ethnic Tutsis who settled in Zaire more than two centuries ago.

Kigali denies the allegations, but independent experts say the Tutsi-dominated armies in both Rwanda and Burundi clearly have a joint interest in pushing the refugees, Hutu guerrilla fighters and genocide leaders out of the area.
"The question is how closely are they cooperating and is the plan to create a buffer zone and nothing more," said one analyst.

Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu on Monday denied his country was giving military help to Tutsi rebels in eastern Zaire, but said he morally supported their struggle against "extermination" by Zairean authorities.

Bizimungu also denied that Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army had been involved in the shelling of Rwandan Hutu refugee camps after failing to persuade the international community to sort out genuine refugees from Hutu genocide leaders.

"We are not supporting the Banyamulenge military. We are not interested in the conquest of land, but people's rights must be respected. The Banyamulenge are entitled to live in Zaire," the president told a news conference at his Kigali office.
"Morally I support their struggle between extermination and survival, I support their resistance against the Zairean authories."

But while Zaire's ailing strongman Mobutu Sese Seko remains out of the country in a private clinic, European politicians increasingly fear the crisis could trigger the long-predicted break-up of Zaire itself.

"The situation is disastrous," Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring told a news conference after a meeting of the 15-nation bloc's foreign ministers in Luxembourg on Monday called for a summit of regional leaders to try and stop the slide to anarchy.
